lines.trans: Viktoriya Sergeyevna, should I bring you a cup of coffee?
Lord, how sick of everything I am!
Have new problems arisen in the restaurant again?
Of course, expensive cognac went missing in the bar.
Bartender Kostya is looking for that bottle now.
Well why does everything always go wrong?
Our work is always very stressful.
The chef shouts, cooks argue, mess everywhere!
You need to rest a bit and calm down.
Can a day really not pass normally?
I am sure everything will work out soon.
I want at least one calm day!
We all want this very much, believe me.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'bar, pub' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Проверьте все бары и старых друзей.
examples.trans: Check all the bars and old friends.
It is already morning. Our bar is closing.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'mess', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: We have a bit of a mess here.
There was total chaos in the room.

examples.text: Извините, у нас тут небольшой бардак.
examples.trans: Excuse us, we have a bit of a mess here.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'bartender', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Бармен, принесите нам бокал белого вина!
examples.trans: Bartender, bring us a glass of white wine!

examples.text: Бармен наливает холодную воду в стакан.
examples.trans: The bartender pours cold water into the glass.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'bottle'.

examples.trans: With a bottle of wine in your hand?

examples.text: Пыталась? С бутылкой вина в руке?
examples.trans: You tried? With a bottle of wine in your hand?

meanings.note: with a past-tense verb: я бы подумал = I would think
wishes: купили бы = we could have bought

examples.text: Я бы на твоём месте подумал.
examples.trans: If I were you, I'd think about it.

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'in' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.
Secondary conversational sense ('into, to') (+ accusative (where to)) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'everywhere'.

examples.trans: Vanya, the water! There's water everywhere!

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.
Secondary conversational sense ('everything') (neuter всё) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('everyone') (plural все) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Prefix 'во-' ('into, up') marks inward or upward movement (stem 'зникнуть'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to arise, emerge', paired with 'возникать'.

examples.text: В ресторане опять возникли новые проблемы?
examples.trans: Have new problems arisen in the restaurant again?

meanings.note: Prefix 'вс-' ('up') marks upward or sudden onset of action (stem 'егда').

examples.trans: She's offended. She's always like that.

meanings.note: ends a conversation or an order: 'Всё, свободен' = that's all, you can go
Secondary conversational sense ('that's it, done') (at the start of a sentence) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: polite to one person, or to several people
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Expressive conversational Russian interjection or greeting ('Good Lord!') used directly in spoken exchanges.
на днях = in the next few days, or the other day

examples.trans: I'll call in the next few days.
Any day now, on the website.

meanings.note: to a loved one, and at the start of letters
to a loved one, and at the start of letters

examples.text: В Москве вам дают деньги на дорогую одежду, а мозги не дают.
examples.trans: In Moscow they give you money for expensive clothes, but they don't give you brains.

достать.gloss: to take out, to get, to reach

meanings.en: to take out, to pull out, to reach
meanings.note: Prefix 'до-' marks reaching a boundary or finishing the remainder of an action (stem 'стать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to take out, to get, to reach', paired with 'доставать'.

meanings.en: to get hold of, to obtain
meanings.note: Secondary conversational sense ('to get hold of, to obtain') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And take his eye out with a spoon.
He took his phone out of his pocket.

examples.text: Вы понимаете, что вы нас достали уже?
examples.trans: Do you understand that you've made us sick of you already?

meanings.note: adds emphasis to the word before it

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: emphasis: вот поэтому ты и... = that's exactly why you...

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to go', forming an aspectual pair with 'пойти'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.
Secondary conversational sense ('expression') (to run for a second term) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: He is running for a second term.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'ис-' ('out from within') marks extraction or exhaustion (stem 'кать'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to look for'.

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'how'.
Secondary conversational sense ('as') (как вы знаете = as you know) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'of course'.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: genitive also 'коньяку' (some cognac)

examples.trans: And you're drinking French cognac yourself.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'coffee', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to shout', forming an aspectual pair with 'крикнуть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Не надо кричать. Хорошо, я буду сегодня.
examples.trans: There's no need to shout. All right, I'll be there tonight.

meanings.note: нас = us (gen/acc/prep); у нас = we have, at our place
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

наладиться.gloss: to work out, get sorted out, improve

meanings.note: всё наладится = everything will work out

examples.trans: Nina, come on, wait! Everything will work out.

meanings.note: наш, наша, наше, наши; agrees with the noun

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: goes right before the word it negates

нельзя.gloss: it is not allowed; one can't

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'it is not allowed'.
Secondary conversational sense ('impossible, can't') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: Not allowed? All right, I'll go and do my homework.

meanings.note: Negative prefix 'не-' ('un-, non-, not') (stem 'много'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'nervous' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.

examples.trans: Do you have a nervous tic?

examples.text: Работа на кухне очень трудная и нервная.
examples.trans: Work in the kitchen is very hard and nerve-wracking.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('really?') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Неужели так трудно найти хороший сюжет?
examples.trans: Is it really so difficult to find a good story?

examples.text: Неужели президент накажет вас за правду?
examples.trans: Will the president really punish you for the truth?
Do you really not care at all?

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('new').

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'fine'.
hesitation, at the start of a sentence
Secondary conversational sense ('oh come on!') (ну, папа!) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
examples.trans: Well, four-eyes? See, there's nothing left.

meanings.en: it is necessary, one needs to
meanings.note: + dative of the person + infinitive: мне нужно позвонить

examples.trans: I need to make a call.

examples.text: Мне нужно позвонить губернатору. Дай телефон.
examples.trans: I need to call the governor. Give me a phone.

meanings.note: agrees in gender and case with the noun
Secondary conversational sense ('alone') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'again'.

examples.text: Нина, не слушай. Это опять обман.
examples.trans: Nina, don't listen. It's another trick.

отдохнуть.gloss: to have a rest; to relax

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'дохнуть'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to have a rest', forming an aspectual pair with 'отдыхать'.
Secondary conversational sense ('to vacation') (to take time off) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: You need to have a proper rest at home.

examples.text: Иди уже скорее домой, пора хорошенько отдохнуть.
examples.trans: Go home already quickly, it is time to have a good rest.

examples.text: Ложись спать, тебе надо хорошо отдохнуть.
examples.trans: Go to sleep, you need to rest well.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'very'.
Secondary conversational sense ('very much') (with verbs: очень люблю) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'cook', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Есть такой английский повар. Я по его передачам научусь готовить.
examples.trans: There is this English chef. I will learn to cook from his shows.

examples.text: Я хочу работать поваром в ресторане.
examples.trans: I want to work as a cook in a restaurant.

meanings.note: + dative of the person: поверить ему

examples.text: Со своего телефона? И все поверили?
examples.trans: From your own phone? And everyone believed it?

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'why'.

examples.trans: Why are we going so slowly?

examples.text: Виталик, почему мы так медленно едем? Быстрее!
examples.trans: Vitalik, why are we going so slowly? Faster!

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'нести'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to bring (carrying)', paired with 'приносить'.

examples.trans: What did you bring into the flat?

examples.text: А я вот вам чаю с сушками принёс.
examples.trans: I've brought you some tea and bread rings.

meanings.note: 'будут проблемы' = there'll be trouble

examples.trans: I know the problems of ordinary people.

пройти.gloss: to go through, to pass; to come along

meanings.note: about a feeling or pain: потом пройдёт = it'll pass
'Пройдёмте' = let's go, an official's polite order

examples.text: Пройдёмте, пожалуйста, за мной к вашему столику у окна.
examples.trans: Please come along with me to your table by the window.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'пасть'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to disappear, vanish'.

examples.text: Аркадий, что делать будем? Самсонов пропал.
examples.trans: Arkady, what are we going to do? Samsonov is missing.

examples.text: Таня, а куда пропал твой бывший муж?
examples.trans: Tanya, and where did your former husband disappear to?

meanings.note: Declinable feminine noun meaning 'work', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.
Secondary conversational sense ('job') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Borrowed from French 'restaurant' (from 'restaurer', to restore strength with rich broth); entered Russian in the early 19th century.

examples.text: Слушай, Нина, это же тот самый ресторан!
examples.trans: Listen, Nina, this is that very restaurant!

examples.text: Мы рады видеть вас в нашем ресторане.
examples.trans: We are glad to see you in our restaurant.
They called from the Italian restaurant.

meanings.note: 'сейчас буду' = I'll be right there
Secondary conversational sense ('in a moment') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'коро'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.text: Так, не шумим. Я скоро вернусь.
examples.trans: Right, no noise. I'll be back soon.

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'calm' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('good (night)') (спокойной ночи = good night) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Это ваша самоуверенность промелькнула. Спокойной ночи!
examples.trans: That was your overconfidence flashing by. Good night!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'порить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to argue, to dispute', paired with 'поспорить'.

examples.trans: That's a nightmare, I don't argue.

examples.text: Это кошмар, я не спорю. Но зачем на видео снимать?
examples.trans: That's a nightmare, I don't argue. But why film it on video?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('so') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or discourse tone in spoken dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('like that, so') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Qualitative or relational adjective formed with the productive '-н-' suffix, meaning 'confident' and agreeing in gender, number, and case.
Secondary conversational sense ('sure, certain') (short form уверен / уверена) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Что-то голос какой-то не очень уверенный.
examples.trans: Your voice doesn't sound very confident.
He answered in a calm, confident voice.

examples.text: Что-то голос какой-то не очень уверенный. Что конкретно?
examples.trans: Your voice doesn't sound very confident. What specifically?

meanings.en: to calm down, to settle down
meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (stem 'спокоиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to calm down', paired with 'успокаиваться'.

Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to want', forming an aspectual pair with 'захотеть'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: нужно хотя бы поговорить = we need at least to talk
Secondary conversational sense ('although, even though (as conjunction)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.text: Нужно хотя бы поговорить с ними.
examples.trans: We need at least to talk with them.

examples.text: Вы плохо поступили, но хотя бы совесть есть.
examples.trans: You acted badly, but at least you have a conscience.

meanings.note: Derived feminine noun formed with a productive Slavic suffix, used in spoken Russian to mean 'cup'.

examples.text: Какое хорошее утро! Лидия Алексеевна, чашку кофе, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: What a lovely morning! Lidia Alekseyevna, a cup of coffee, please.

meanings.note: + past tense: 'чтобы свидетели были'
Secondary conversational sense ('in order to') (+ infinitive) used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm calling to say thank you.
So that there are witnesses, Samson.

meanings.note: Borrowed from French 'chef' (head, leader, from Latin 'caput'); in Russian kitchen culture 'шеф' is the standard form of address for the executive head chef.

examples.trans: The chef is in the kitchen.

meanings.note: pointing at a thing or a situation; 'это' + noun = 'this is ...'
points at something: это моё = that's mine
Secondary conversational sense ('is') (linking word: главное — это народ) used in spoken Russian dialogue.
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:') used in spoken Russian dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you. A toy car!

meanings.note: alone: 'я этого не хочу' = I don't want that

examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat.

examples.text: Меня уже тошнит от этой коммуналки! У нас труба уже неделю течёт.
examples.trans: I'm sick of this communal flat! Our pipe has been leaking for a week now.

meanings.note: меня = me (genitive/accusative), мне = to me (dative)
Secondary conversational sense ('other forms:  (gen/acc),  (dat),  (instr),  (prep)') used in spoken Russian dialogue.
